_comment: Post-mission disposal rules, with provenance. V2_BRIEF.md §3 states the
five-year rule but explicitly says not to treat that paragraph as
authoritative, so each rule here was checked against its own source and
the wording that actually matters is recorded verbatim.
Two corrections to the brief's summary came out of that check:
1. The five-year clock starts at END OF MISSION, not at launch. A
satellite with a 7-year design life at 705 km has 12 years from
2. The FCC rule is scoped to disposal by UNCONTROLLED atmospheric
re-entry from below 2000 km. Controlled de-orbit and re-orbit to a
disposal orbit are different paths with different requirements.
Nothing here is a physics constant. These are legal thresholds that
change; they live in data/ so a rule change is a data edit, not a code
edit, and so the compliance verdict can name the rule it applied.

rules.label: FCC 5-year rule
rules.quote: For space stations ending their mission in or passing through the low-Earth orbit region below 2000 km altitude and planning disposal through uncontrolled atmospheric re-entry, disposal must be completed as soon as practicable following end of mission, and no later than five years after the end of the mission.
rules.effective_note: Binding on applications filed on or after this date; two-year transition from adoption.

rules.label: IADC 25-year guideline
rules.citation: IADC Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines; ISO 24113
rules.quote: Long-standing international guideline that objects passing through LEO be removed from orbit within 25 years of end of mission.
rules.effective_note: Non-binding guideline. Superseded in US practice by the FCC rule above, still the reference elsewhere and the baseline most published designs were sized against.
rules.confidence_note: Widely reported and uncontroversial, but the 25-year figure is quoted here from secondary summaries rather than read out of the IADC document itself.
